notes: Trustee appeal on s375 rescission of trust declaration over PDQ receipts; Laddie J restores June order and examination.

enrichment.short_title: Papanicola v Humphreys: s375 rescission and bankrupt restaurant credit card receipts
key_facts: Trustee in bankruptcy Samuel Sing Kee Mak continued to run the Ugly Duckling restaurant after his bankruptcy and entered a PDQ contract with Readygame Ltd.
Readygame received £50,361.83 in credit card receipts between March and September 2003; District Judge Blomfield held Readygame liable for £50,000 to the Trustee.
Registrar Rawson initially declared the sums held on trust for the bankrupt estate but rescinded that order in November 2004, treating the receipts as post-bankruptcy income of Mr Mak.
Mr Humphreys did not attend the June hearing and later applied under section 375 to rescind the trust declaration.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to Laddie J against a registrar's November 2004 order rescinding an earlier declaration that Readygame held credit card receipts on trust for the bankrupt estate.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; November order set aside; section 375 rescission held unavailable without exceptional circumstances and new material.
enrichment.ratio: Section 375 gives a wide discretion to review insolvency orders but may be exercised only in exceptional circumstances where something materially new justifies reconsideration; a party who deliberately absented himself from the earlier hearing must explain non-attendance and act promptly, and cannot simply re-argue the same case more effectively.
legal_issues: Whether section 375 permits rescission absent exceptional circumstances
Whether restaurant credit card receipts were estate property or post-bankruptcy income requiring an income payments order
Whether Mr Humphreys was estopped by the earlier judgment against Readygame
Whether non-attendance at the original hearing could itself constitute new material
linked_authorities: Fitch v Official Receiver [1996] 1 WLR 242
Re R S & M Engineering Co Ltd [1999] 2 BCLC 485
In re A Debtor (No 32 of 1991) [1993] 1 WLR 314

confidence.notes: Section 375 analysis, factual chronology and allowance of appeal are clearly reasoned.

notes: Short leap-frog procedural order; Court of Appeal dismissed appeal by consent and granted HL leave with costs to follow.

enrichment.short_title: Botham v MoD: leap-frog leave to House of Lords granted by consent
key_facts: The Court of Appeal heard an application relating to Botham v Ministry of Defence alongside a carbon-copy case in which the House of Lords had already granted leave.
The appeal was dismissed by consent while leave to appeal to the House of Lords was granted as a leap-frog remedy.
The appellant was legally aided and sought guidance on costs where the appeal was dismissed by consent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application in the Court of Appeal for leave to leap-frog to the House of Lords in a case paralleling an existing appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed by consent; leave to appeal to the House of Lords granted; costs to follow the result of the House of Lords appeal with community legal services assessment.
enrichment.ratio: Where their Lordships have already granted leave in an essentially identical case, the Court of Appeal may grant leap-frog leave without inferentially holding the decision under appeal wrong; costs may follow the ultimate result in the House of Lords despite consent dismissal.
legal_issues: Whether leap-frog leave to the House of Lords should be granted
Appropriate costs order where the Court of Appeal appeal is dismissed by consent but HL leave is granted
Treatment of legally aided appellant's costs

confidence.notes: Procedural order only; substantive merits were not adjudicated.

notes: Day nursery planning s288 challenge dismissed; Richards J holds inspector adequately considered conditions and outdoor play noise.

enrichment.short_title: Shinh v SoS: planning challenge to refusal of Hinckley day nursery expansion
key_facts: Claimants operated a day nursery at a house in Hinckley with permission for up to 24 children and sought to expand to 35 including first-floor use.
Hinckley and Bosworth Borough Council refused the application and an inspector dismissed the appeal, finding outdoor play would materially harm neighbours' living conditions.
Claimants offered section 106/play-management restrictions limiting garden use to one hour per session and eight children at a time.
The inspector held such conditions would be difficult to enforce and that overall numbers should not increase.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under section 288 of the 1990 Act challenging an inspector's dismissal of a planning appeal by written representations.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed on all three grounds; inspector's reasoning on conditions, childcare standards and noise findings upheld.
enrichment.ratio: An inspector who considers proposed planning conditions and explains why garden play restrictions would be unworkable and unenforceable gives adequate reasons; assessment of outdoor nursery noise is a matter of professional judgment and need not rely on technical noise measurements.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector failed adequately to consider imposing conditions instead of refusal
Whether childcare standards were an irrelevant consideration
Whether adverse noise findings were unreasonable without expert measurement evidence
linked_authorities: South Buckinghamshire District Council v Porter [2004] UKHL 33
Westminster Renslade Ltd v Secretary of State for the Environment [1984] 48 P&CR 255

confidence.notes: Three grounds, inspector reasoning and dismissal are comprehensively analysed.

notes: Asylum appeal restored; Laws LJ holds IAT exceeded s101 jurisdiction on nationality and helicopter credibility findings.

enrichment.short_title: Rusiga v SSHD: IAT exceeded jurisdiction on Burundian asylum credibility
key_facts: Burundian Hutu appellant claimed persecution after attacks linked to her husband's suspected rebel activity, including rape and her husband's disappearance.
The adjudicator found her credible and a Burundian national despite speaking only Swahili and giving a rough 30-minute helicopter journey estimate from Bujumbura to Entebbe.
The IAT allowed the Secretary of State's appeal, holding inability to speak Kirundi meant she could not be Burundian and that the helicopter account was perverse.
The Secretary of State conceded the IAT did not identify an error of law and accepted remittal, but the Court of Appeal restored the adjudicator outright.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision allowing the Secretary of State's appeal from an adjudicator's asylum determination promulgated after 9 June 2003.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; adjudicator's decision restored; no remittal because the IAT had no legitimate jurisdiction to substitute its own evaluation.
enrichment.ratio: After commencement of section 101 of the 2002 Act, the IAT may interfere with an adjudicator's factual findings only where they disclose an error of law such as Wednesbury perversity or inadequate reasons; a mistaken helicopter timing estimate and disputed language evidence did not meet that threshold.
legal_issues: Scope of IAT jurisdiction under section 101 after 9 June 2003
Whether inability to speak Kirundi made a finding of Burundian nationality perverse
Whether acceptance of a 30-minute helicopter journey estimate was irrational
Whether remittal to a differently constituted tribunal was appropriate
linked_authorities: CA v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] EWCA Civ 1165
Karanakaran v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2000] IAR 271

confidence.notes: Statutory jurisdiction issue and restoration of adjudicator are clearly reasoned by the full court.

notes: Gloster J grants summary judgment on 24-month fraudulent receivables policy time bar; waiver and estoppel rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Fortisbank v Trenwick: summary judgment on fraudulent receivables policy time bar
key_facts: Fortisbank sued underwriters on a fraudulent receivables policy after Zye Technology invoice discounting fraud discovered in February 2000.
Fortis notified underwriters on 11 February 2000 that invoices had been issued without delivery and credit notes withheld; a quantified £1 million claim was asserted by May 2000.
Proceedings were not issued until 23 July 2003, outside General Condition 13(b)'s 24 months from discovery.
Fortis argued waiver, estoppel or implied agreement that underwriters would not rely on the limitation clause during prolonged claim negotiations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court summary judgment application under CPR Part 24 on contractual limitation and strike-out/debarring applications.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment for underwriters; loss discovered by February 2000 at latest; no real prospect of defeating the time bar by waiver, promissory estoppel or estoppel by convention.
enrichment.ratio: Discovery under the policy occurred when Fortis became aware of facts causing a reasonable person to assume covered loss, which happened in February 2000; negotiations and reservations of rights do not amount to an unequivocal promise not to rely on a contractual limitation clause.
legal_issues: When Fortis discovered the insured loss under General Condition 18
Whether correspondence amounted to waiver or promissory estoppel of the 24-month time bar
Whether estoppel by convention prevented reliance on Condition 13(b)
Effect of breach of a consent order on Fortis's Reply pleading
linked_authorities: Seechurn v Ace [2002] 2 Lloyd's Rep 390
The Kanchenjunga [1991] 1 Lloyd's Rep 391
HIH Casualty and General Insurance Ltd v AXA Corporate Solutions [2003] 1 Lloyd's Rep IR 1

confidence.notes: Discovery timing, Seechurn principles and summary judgment disposition are detailed and explicit.

notes: Long s459 unfair prejudice trial; Mrs Fisher succeeds on several grounds and buy-out ordered in principle.

enrichment.short_title: Fisher v Cadman: unfair prejudice petition in family property company
key_facts: Mrs Fisher held about one-third of Cadman Developments Ltd, a property company founded by her father James Cadman, alongside brothers Cedric and Rodney.
Relations broke down after family deaths and disputes over dividends, management information, related-company transactions and property portfolio strategy.
Mrs Fisher petitioned under sections 459 and 461 for relief or alternatively just and equitable winding up.
The judge found unfair prejudice on several grounds but rejected allegations of property mismanagement and director deadlock.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of a petition for unfairly prejudicial conduct relief under the Companies Act 1985 with alternative winding-up claim.
enrichment.outcome: Petition partly successful; buy-out of Mrs Fisher's shares ordered in principle with precise terms to be addressed separately; winding up not ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Minority shareholders may obtain a buy-out where conduct of majority directors is unfairly prejudicial and continuation of shareholding is intolerable; holding a long-term property portfolio without refurbishment is not necessarily mismanagement if within a band of reasonable commercial decisions.
legal_issues: Whether dividends, remuneration and related-party transactions were unfairly prejudicial
Whether failure to distribute or develop the property portfolio amounted to mismanagement
Whether deadlock between the Cadman brothers justified relief
Appropriate remedy under section 461
linked_authorities: Re Bird Precision Bellows Ltd [1984] Ch 419
Re Macro (Ipswich) Ltd [1994] 2 BCLC 354

confidence.notes: Outcome and several key findings are clear though the judgment is lengthy and remedial terms were reserved.

notes: Wilson J remits overage valuation after master wrongly resorted to burden of proof; supplemental agreement construction upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Stephens v Cannon: overage damages and burden of proof on valuation
key_facts: Sellers sold Surrey land for £600,000 with overage requiring buyers to pay 50% of sale proceeds above £1 million after building and selling a new dwelling.
Buyers obtained planning permission but never built; sellers obtained damages for breach of the overage condition.
A Supplemental Agreement provided overage applied only after the Bank of Ireland charge was repaid from net proceeds.
Master Price adopted the buyers' £1.5m valuation by resort to the burden of proof after unable to choose between expert valuers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from a master's assessment of damages for breach of an overage condition in a land sale contract.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on valuation; damages award set aside and valuation remitted to a High Court judge; cross-appeal on mortgage deduction construction dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: A court may despatch a disputed issue by the burden of proof only in exceptional cases after striving to decide it and explaining why decision is impossible; the Supplemental Agreement prioritised the bank's charge over overage but did not deduct borrowings from the overage calculation threshold.
legal_issues: Construction of overage and Supplemental Agreement as to Bank of Ireland deductions
When a tribunal may resort to the burden of proof on expert valuation evidence
Whether the master demonstrated he strove to resolve conflicting surveyor evidence
Appropriate remittal procedure for reassessment of damages
linked_authorities: Rhesa Shipping Co SA v Edmunds [1985] 1 WLR 948
Sewell v Electrolux Ltd (The Times, 7 November 1997)
Morris v London Iron and Steel Co Ltd [1988] QB 493

confidence.notes: Detailed burden-of-proof analysis and supplemental agreement construction are fully reasoned.

notes: Fresh asylum claim JR dismissed; Hughes J holds medical report was available before IAT and para 346 applied.

enrichment.short_title: R v SSHD: refusal to treat Uganda twins' further representations as fresh claim
key_facts: Ugandan twin sisters claimed asylum based on UPDF and ADF violence linked to their brother and father; initial claims were refused and appeals dismissed for non-attendance.
First solicitors wrote that they were without instructions; a Medical Foundation report corroborating rape scars was available by late July 2003 but not submitted to the IAT.
Third solicitors asked the Home Secretary in February 2004 to treat further representations as a fresh claim relying on the medical evidence and solicitor negligence.
The Secretary of State refused under paragraph 346 of HC395, finding the material was previously available and not sufficiently different.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's refusal under paragraph 346 of the Immigration Rules to treat further representations as a fresh asylum claim.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; medical report was available before the IAT determination; no Wednesbury unreasonableness in treating solicitor failures as barring a fresh claim.
enrichment.ratio: Under paragraph 346, material available at the time of refusal or final appeal determination is excluded from consideration; limited corroborative medical evidence does not justify treating a substantially unchanged asylum claim as fresh even where successive solicitors may have been negligent.
legal_issues: Whether the Medical Foundation report was available when previous appeals were determined
Application of paragraph 346 and Onibiyo/Ladd v Marshall criteria
Relevance of solicitors' negligence to fresh claim decisions
Whether exceptional circumstances justified departure from paragraph 346
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex parte Onibiyo [1996] QB 768
Al-Mehdawi v Secretary of State for the Home Department [1990] 1 AC 876
E & R v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] QB 1004

confidence.notes: Chronology, paragraph 346 analysis and dismissal are comprehensively reasoned.

notes: Steria appeal dismissed on selected grounds; contract was £200k implementation services not full install; waiver upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Peregrine v Steria: IT software licence dispute and waiver of termination
key_facts: Peregrine licensed call-centre software to Steria under a 2002 agreement with £800,000 licence fees and £200,000 optional implementation services.
Steria terminated on 5 February 2003 alleging repudiatory breaches; Peregrine claimed £700,000 due and the TCC judge gave judgment for Peregrine.
Steria appealed on 23 grounds but the court heard only tardy performance and waiver issues.
The Technical Services Schedule provided time-and-materials implementation up to £200,000, not completion of full installation by a fixed date.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Technology and Construction Court trial judgment on a software licence and implementation services contract.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on the two issues heard; no repudiatory breach on implementation timing and Steria waived any right to terminate.
enrichment.ratio: A technical services schedule for £200,000 of time-and-materials implementation did not oblige the supplier to complete full software installation within a reasonable time once the budget was exhausted; continued use of licensed software and pursuit of revised commercial terms amounted to election to affirm the contract.
legal_issues: Whether Peregrine contractually undertook to complete full software implementation
Whether delay amounted to a repudiatory breach of a reasonable time obligation
Whether Steria waived the right to terminate by continuing to use the software and negotiate
Distinction between breach of reasonable time and time being of the essence
linked_authorities: Hongkong Fir Shipping Co Ltd v Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha Ltd [1962] 2 QB 26
The Kanchenjunga [1990] 1 Lloyd's Rep 391
Astea (UK) Ltd v Time Group Ltd [2003] EWHC 725

confidence.notes: Contract construction and waiver findings on the selected issues are detailed though most appeal grounds were not heard.

notes: Mackenzie Friend rights of audience refused for struck-off solicitor partner; parity between litigants in person.

enrichment.short_title: Re D: refusal of rights of audience to struck-off solicitor Mackenzie Friend
key_facts: Mrs Francis, a litigant in person and legal secretary, sought rights of audience for her partner Mr Ty Francis to act as her Mackenzie Friend.
Mr Francis was a solicitor struck off the roll by the Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal.
Black J had previously allowed him to speak at an without-notice hearing where no objection was taken.
The respondent former husband, also a litigant in person, objected on fairness grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal/refuse rights of audience for a Mackenzie Friend in family proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; exceptional grant of rights of audience under sections 27 and 28 not justified for a struck-off solicitor where both parties were litigants in person.
enrichment.ratio: Courts may grant rights of audience to a Mackenzie Friend only in exceptional circumstances after careful consideration; where both parties are litigants in person, fairness and parity preclude granting audience to a struck-off solicitor partner even if he could present the case more effectively.
legal_issues: Whether exceptional circumstances justified granting rights of audience to a Mackenzie Friend
Effect of a prior without-notice order allowing the friend to speak
Fairness between litigants in person when one seeks professional assistance from a disqualified lawyer

confidence.notes: Short procedural ruling; statutory framework and refusal grounds are clearly stated.
